opus-5.5.text:
I think what excites me most about in-context learning is that it changes the relationship between us and the model. Traditionally, if you wanted a neural network to do something new, you had to collect a dataset, define a loss, and run gradient descent, so the only real lever you had was the training process itself. With in-context learning, you can teach the model a new task just by showing it a few examples or describing what you want in natural language, and it adapts on the fly without any weight updates. That makes the interaction feel much more like communication than like engineering.

It's also exciting because it opens up the space of what we can ask these models to do. A lot of my work has been around algorithmic reasoning, things like teaching models to do multi-digit addition or follow a procedure step by step. What we found is that if you're very explicit in the prompt about the algorithm, spelling out each step and the rules for handling things like carries, the model can follow it much more reliably and generalize to longer problems than it could from just seeing input-output pairs. So the prompt becomes a kind of program you're writing for the model, except the programming language is natural language plus demonstrations.

And from a scientific perspective, I find it fascinating that this ability emerges at all. Nobody explicitly trained these models to learn from context; it seems to fall out of pretraining at scale. Understanding what the model is actually doing when it learns in context, whether it's retrieving something it already knows, composing skills, or doing something closer to genuine learning, tells us a lot about how these models represent knowledge. So it's both a very practical tool and a really rich research question, and that combination is what keeps me coming back to it.

r001.rationale: It says a model can be taught a new task by showing examples, and discusses learning from input–output pairs in the prompt.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the model adapts to a new task without any weight updates.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what excites me about in-context learning is that it's a fundamentally different way of getting a model to do something new. Traditionally, if you wanted a model to learn a task, you had to change its weights. You'd collect data, run gradient descent, and the knowledge ended up baked into the parameters. With in-context learning, you don't touch the weights at all. You just put a few examples, or a description of the task, into the prompt, and the model adapts on the fly.

That's exciting to me for a couple of reasons. One is that it's much closer to how we interact with people. If I want a colleague to help me with something, I don't retrain them. I explain the task, maybe show them an example or two, and they figure it out. Being able to do that with a model lowers the barrier enormously. You don't need a dataset, you don't need a training pipeline, you just need to be able to describe what you want.

The other reason is more scientific. In-context learning is a bit mysterious. It emerges from training on next-token prediction, nobody explicitly designed it, and yet the model is doing something that looks a lot like learning inside a single forward pass. So there's this interesting question of what algorithm the model is actually implementing when it does that. Is it doing something like retrieval over patterns it saw in pretraining? Is it approximating some kind of gradient step internally? Understanding that tells us something about what these models really are.

And then practically, it opens up this whole space of instructions and prompting as a kind of programming. You can give the model a procedure in natural language, and it will try to follow it. The fact that this works at all, and that it keeps getting better as models scale, suggests we're only at the beginning of figuring out how to communicate with these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can adapt from examples placed in the prompt and figure out the task.

r002.rationale: It explicitly states that in-context learning does not touch or change the model's weights.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that you can teach the model what you want through examples, without updating its parameters. You put a few demonstrations into the context, and the model can often pick up the pattern and apply it to a new input. So the prompt becomes a way of specifying a task, even when that task would be difficult to describe precisely in words.

That makes it a very accessible way to interact with these models. But it also raises a fascinating research question: what is the model actually learning from those examples? Is it recognizing a task it has seen during training, or figuring out a new relationship from the information in the context? Understanding that distinction can tell us a lot about both the capabilities and the limitations of language models.

r001.rationale: It says the model can pick up a pattern from demonstrations in context and apply it to a new input.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says examples can teach the model what to do without updating its parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that you can change what a model does just by changing the context you give it. You can describe a task, show a few examples, and then ask it to apply that pattern to a new input—all without updating its parameters. That makes it a very flexible way to interact with a model, because you’re expressing what you want in language rather than building a separate training pipeline.

It also raises a really interesting scientific question: what is the model actually doing with those examples? Is it recognizing a task it already knows, or learning something new from the context? Understanding that distinction could tell us a lot about how these models generalize.

r001.rationale: It says you can show the model a few examples and ask it to apply that pattern to a new input, clearly describing inference from prompt examples.

r002.rationale: It states this can happen “without updating its parameters,” directly conveying that prompting elicits behavior without changing the model’s weights.
